title: def and defaults
summary: Define functions, return values, and dodge the mutable default trap.

steps.title: def
body: print(area(height=4, width=3))  # keyword arguments, any order
- No return type or parameter types are required (type hints come in module 5).
- The string right under `def` is a **docstring**, Python's `/// <summary>`.
- Functions are objects: you can store them in variables and pass them around.

steps.explain: `greet` prints but returns nothing, so `result` is `None`. Assigning `greet` to `say` copies the reference to the function.

steps.title: Clamp
prompt: Write `clamp(value, low, high)` that returns `value` limited to the range `low..high`.
**Run checks** calls your function with several values.

steps.title: Default values
body: Parameters can have defaults, as in C#:
greet("Bo", punct="?")       # skip one by naming the other
Unlike C#, defaults can be any expression, **but it is evaluated once, when `def` runs**, not on every call. That matters a lot for mutable defaults.

steps.explain: The default list is created **once** and shared by every call that does not pass a basket. This is the most famous Python trap.

steps.title: The fix: None as the default
body: Use `None` as a sentinel and create the fresh object inside:
The same applies to `{}`, `set()` and any object you mutate. Immutable defaults (`0`, `""`, `None`, tuples) are safe.

steps.explain: Only mutable defaults are shared dangerously. Ints, strings and tuples cannot be changed in place.

steps.title: Fix the shared default
prompt: `log(message, history=...)` should append the message to `history` and return it. Called without a history, it must start a **new** list every time.
The tests call `log("a")` and then `log("b")` and expect `["b"]` the second time.
template: Dojo.eq("log('y', mine) appends to mine", ["x", "y"], log("y", mine))
Dojo.check("returns the same list it was given", log("z", mine) is mine, "should return the list passed in")

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a function that returns both the minimum and maximum of a list.

steps.title: Word counter function
prompt: Write `count_words(text, ignore=None)` that returns a dict of lowercase word to count, in first-seen order. `ignore` is an optional collection of words to skip (compare in lowercase).
solution: ignore = {w.lower() for w in ignore} if ignore else set()
template: Dojo.eq("counts words", {"the": 2, "cat": 1, "hat": 1}, count_words("The cat the hat"))
Dojo.eq("ignores words", {"cat": 1, "hat": 1}, count_words("The cat the hat", {"the"}))
Dojo.eq("ignore list is case-insensitive", {"b": 1}, count_words("a B", ["A"]))
Dojo.eq("keeps first-seen order", ["z", "a"], list(count_words("z a z")))
hints: Default `ignore` to `None`, then turn it into a set of lowercase words.
